about-me.title: about me
about-me.text:
Hi! I’m Riva. 

You’ve gotten this far and now I consider us friends. It’s nice to meet you! I’ll keep this as a short, unofficial introduction for now. I’ve wanted to start a blog for the longest time, but was afraid of it not being all polished and “perfect”. After a lot of back and forth though, I finally decided to just go for it.

This site originally started as a space for my art, specifically, the kind of art that’s meant to be lived with, not just admired from afar. You’ll still find plenty of art-related posts here (because it’s a big part of me), but I’ve expanded the scope to share all the random things I find fascinating, the cool things I’ve learned, and just the thoughts that pop up in my head. It’s a mix of everything I love and care about.

So, yeah, this site is a little chaotic, but I promise I’ll keep it organized enough for you to enjoy. Thanks for stopping by, and I hope you find something that sparks your curiosity! :’)

When I’m not busy with classes or creating something new, I’m out and about on campus or involved in projects that allow me to channel my passions into action. Every part of my life is an extension of my creativity, and I hope this site reflects that!

Feel free to reach out, share your thoughts, or just say hello. I’d love to hear from you and learn what you’re passionate about, too!

sos.title: sos
sos.text:
sos 

Hi! Welcome to SOS (aka my shiny object syndrome hehe) where I dump all the little things I’ve learned—fun facts, insights, and anything else that’s caught my attention. Essentially, think of it as a space to explore random but interesting bits of knowledge, and who knows? Maybe you’ll find something that sparks your interest! Enjoy!

This probably isn’t of use to you guys, but I’ve made it a mission to be able to name all 196 countries! So far I’ve improved from knowing 34 to 149…

I absolutely love Herpetology— the study of amphibians and reptiles. I would study it religiously and won a national award for this, want to lowkey get back into it.

side-quests-2.title: Side Quests
side-quests-2.text:
Side Quests

Let’s face it, I’m a sucker for shiny objects. Whether it’s a new idea, a fun side project, or a challenge, I tend to try a little bit of everything. It’s my way of learning, growing, and having fun along the way. These “side quests” may not be the core of my work, but they’ve helped me expand my skill set, connect with new people, and explore areas I never would have otherwise. Take a look at some of the cool things I’ve dipped my toes into—who knows, maybe they’ll inspire you to start your own side quest!

The Riva Gallery!! (duh) 

Starting this blog has been the perfect creative outlet for me. It’s like me wrapped up in a little corner of the internet—everything I’m learning, the books I’m reading, my art, and whatever else is on my mind. There’s no pressure, just a place where I can let my thoughts and creativity flow freely. It’s all about sharing what inspires me, and I love how it all comes together, no matter how random it gets.

ai-consulting-unc.text:
AI Consulting @ UNC

As the Marketing Director for the AI Consulting Club, I handle all aspects of member communication and content creation. I manage the club’s social media platforms, creating engaging content that highlights club events, updates, and industry trends. I also facilitate communication between club members, ensuring everyone is informed and engaged in club activities. Additionally, I help promote collaborative initiatives, ensuring that the club’s outreach resonates with both current and potential members, while fostering a strong, informed community of AI enthusiasts. Examples below:

 View this post on Instagram

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

I’m also leading the planning and execution of our 2025 AI Consulting Case Competition. My responsibilities include designing the marketing and promotional materials, coordinating logistics such as all email communications, forming teams, handling forms and organization, booking rooms, teams, sending emails, and handling forms. I also work closely with another executive board member to design the case itself, creating a case deck that integrates both quantitative and qualitative data. the-big-leaf-safe-start.title: The Big Leaf – Safe Start
the-big-leaf-safe-start.text:
The Big Leaf – Safe Start

Healthcare Startup Consulting Through Executive Consulting Firm

This summer, I’ll be consulting for Safe Start, a healthcare startup, founded by a surgeon, focused on preventing “never events” in surgery, through The Big Leaf, an executive consulting firm based in Toronto. In this role, I’ll help Safe Start refine its strategic approach to improve patient safety and surgical outcomes. I will also be conducting market research and analyzing industry trends to identify competitive opportunities, while contributing to the development of marketing strategies aimed at increasing adoption and brand awareness. Additionally, I’ll be working on business development initiatives, including fostering strategic partnerships to accelerate growth and impact in the healthcare sector.

case-competitions.title: Case Competitions
case-competitions.text:
Case Competitions

There’s no mistake this section comes first—I love case competitions. Seriously, I’m a case competition fanatic. There’s something about the fast-paced problem-solving, high-stakes presentations, and strategic thinking that makes case competitions feel like the varsity sport of the business world. It’s where creativity meets strategy, where bold ideas get put to the test, and honestly, where I have the most fun.

P&G Case Competition – 1st Place

Won 1st place (of 38 teams) by developing a standout recommendation for Crest.

Created two new product innovations and a functional prototype of an app that connected all recommendations.

Designed a marketing strategy focused on brand loyalty and customer acquisition.

Formulated a sales and market share growth strategy based on competitive analysis and consumer insights.

Presented directly to the Global Senior VP of Crest ($1.5B brand).

KPMG Case Competition – 1st Place

Consulted a regional bank and developed strategic initiatives to increase market share.

Created niche, high-impact recommendations that set our team apart. 

Enhanced the bank’s current mobile app through fintech partnerships, demonstrating this through a functional prototype. 

National Women’s Case Competition (UT Austin) – Semifinalists

Hosted by Apple, this competition brought together 27 teams from across the country.

Placed as semifinalists, presenting innovative recommendations in a highly competitive field.

PwC Case Competition – 2nd Place

Competed at the annual PwC Case Competition, placing 2nd among several teams.

Designed an app prototype as part of our innovative solution.

Developed a marketing strategy to improve employee retention.

CSF Case Competition (Midterm) 

Part of the Consulting Skills & Frameworks course, focused on applying structured problem-solving methodologies.

Tasked with increasing student engagement for UNC’s Rams Club, an organization that funds scholarships and resources for UNC student-athletes.

Identified untapped student markets, creating an innovative approach to expand revenue and boost student involvement.

Other Case Competitions:

Hurricanes Case Competition

Deloitte Case Competition

consult-your-community.title: Consult Your Community
consult-your-community.text:
Consult Your Community

UNC Global Affairs

With my team, I consulted for UNC Global Affairs to develop and refine the Carolina Diplomacy Fellows program. We conducted competitive analysis, designed tiered incentives, and implemented strategies to enhance inclusivity. We led market research through surveys and club partnerships, crafted a marketing plan with a social media content calendar, redesigned the program’s logo, and developed feedback mechanisms for continuous improvement. We supported the program’s beta launch by assessing student sentiment and providing data-driven recommendations for future expansion. 

Undergraduate Real Estate Club

With my team, I led key initiatives to strengthen engagement and professional development within the Undergraduate Real Estate Club. We designed and launched a mentorship program to connect underclassmen with upperclassmen, providing industry guidance, networking opportunities, and a way to keep upperclassmen involved in the club. Additionally, I played a major role in organizing the club’s internal case competition. This involved securing sponsorships from local real estate firms, designing outreach materials, coordinating event logistics, and developing the case itself. We worked to ensure the competition provided a hands-on learning experience that encouraged innovative problem-solving and industry exposure for participants.

books.title: books
books.text:
book reviews 

I post some of the books I read on Instagram, but I can’t really say much with 2,000 people watching—so it’s usually limited to just a numerical rating, how it made me feel, and a quote or two that hit.

But here’s the full yaps. SPOILERS ALERT!! 

9/10 

I watched the movie a year before reading the book, but even knowing the plot, the book still surprised me. Snow’s inner thoughts reveal just how complex and cunning he is—and what leads to his downfall. It made me wonder what I’d do in his shoes, considering his circumstances. Even knowing the ending, I was on edge the whole time. If you liked the movie, the book is definitely more intense and worth the read.

10/10

This is a beautiful Japanese novel of two novellas about love, loss, and healing. It offered a fresh perspective beyond the Western books I usually read. Her simple, powerful writing captures heartbreak and resilience, with memorable quotes about accepting life’s hardships and the strength of non-family bonds. I love that the novel shows you that you should consider yourself lucky if you have someone in your life that makes saying goodbye hard. Highly recommend. Quotes:

“I realized that the world did not exist for my benefit. It followed that the ratio of pleasant and unpleasant things around me would not change. It wasn’t up to me. It was clear that the best thing to do was to adopt a sort of muddled cheerfulness.”

“People aren’t overcome by situations or outside forces; defeat invades from within.”

“But it won’t hurt so much if you just accept it as a part of life”

“It was the mystery of being close to someone who is not family.”

10/10

The structure was a bit confusing at first but everything clicked by the end. It really hits you with the idea that you might not get another day, so you should make every moment count—not in a morbid way, just live a good story. What stuck with me most is how two strangers, knowing their time is limited, manage to build something real anyway. It makes you think about how you spend your time, and who you spend it with.

5/10

The behavioral economics concepts are fascinating and insightful, but I found many of the experiments poorly designed or biased, which weakened the arguments. The book often focuses too much on experimental details rather than unpacking the implications or addressing limitations. It’s an interesting read overall, but could have been stronger with clearer explanations and more critical reflection on the research.

10/10

This book takes place during the 50th Hunger Games (aka the one Haymitch won) and somehow connects all the dots from the other books to make everything way worse, but in the best way possible. Everything you think you know about the Capitol is actually ten times worse.

I literally read it in one sitting. I didn’t move from the couch all day and even read while eating. And I was in tears by the end. 

8/10

The title definitely holds true. The ideas aren’t brand new, but the book frames them in totally new ways. This was my second time reading it, and obviously more of it stuck, especially if you’re into the whole “harsh reality” of things (which I am sometimes). I gave it an 8/10 because it’s well-written and thought-provoking, even if I didn’t agree with everything.
Favorite essay: #36

If you’re interested, I wrote more about essay #12 on my blog about the knowing-doing gap. 

6/10

The ending with James and the last call actually made me cry, but overall I’d give it a 6. The plot was okay, focusing on Julie’s life after Sam’s death. I’m lucky not to have experienced true grief yet, so while I know it’s inevitable, I’m not sure I’m built for that kind of deep pain. Julie’s grieving felt real but didn’t dive too deep, so it didn’t fully hit me or have the same impact it might for someone going through loss. Still, it’s a sweet story for anyone dealing with grief.

7.5/10

The ending was bittersweet. I liked the storyline and the title was intriguing, but it could have been developed more. Joseph’s time with Jack’s family was detailed but didn’t have much impact. I wish we learned more about his time in juvie, his dad, or his journey with Madeline. The ending felt rushed, and it would have been nice to see Jupiter’s perspective later or switch between Jack’s and Madeline’s viewpoints.

8/10
I reread Hatchet after eight years because it randomly came to mind. It was the first book that ever made me sob, especially when the pilot died. Although some quotes hit a bit too bluntly for my taste, I still love them.

“…he learned the most important rule of survival, which was that feeling sorry for yourself didn’t work.” 

“You are your most valuable asset. Don’t forget that. You are the best thing you have.” 

10/10

10/10

This is a powerful reminder to notice the everyday things we usually overlook. Using the story of two fish unaware of the water around them, Wallace challenges us to step out of autopilot and choose how we see the world. I wrote more about how this speech resonated with me during a high school class (and later again in a college class) in my blog post here: (about water). 

9.5/10

7/10

I gave the Harry Potter series a 7 out of 10. I binge-read all the books in a week, and while I enjoyed the magical world and characters, some parts felt dragged out or overhyped. It was fun to experience but didn’t totally wow me like I expected.

9/10

Beyond the action, it’s a sharp look at power, control, and survival. The Capitol’s use of media feels all too real, and Katniss’s struggle is about more than just survival, it’s about identity and resisting oppression. The story digs into trauma, morality, and inequality in a way that stuck with me long after reading.

6.5/10

Congrats on making it to the end! I definitely read way more in middle school, but unfortunately I’ve forgotten all of it — plus, you’ve probably already read those books anyway. You know the gist.

If you’ve got any recs for me though, send them my way 🙂

“People aren’t overcome by situations or outside forces; defeat invades from within.”

“But it won’t hurt so much if you just accept it as a part of life”

“It was the mystery of being close to someone who is not family.”

10/10

The structure was a bit confusing at first but everything clicked by the end. It really hits you with the idea that you might not get another day, so you should make every moment count—not in a morbid way, just live a good story. What stuck with me most is how two strangers, knowing their time is limited, manage to build something real anyway. It makes you think about how you spend your time, and who you spend it with.

5/10

The behavioral economics concepts are fascinating and insightful, but I found many of the experiments poorly designed or biased, which weakened the arguments. The book often focuses too much on experimental details rather than unpacking the implications or addressing limitations. It’s an interesting read overall, but could have been stronger with clearer explanations and more critical reflection on the research.

10/10

This book takes place during the 50th Hunger Games (aka the one Haymitch won) and somehow connects all the dots from the other books to make everything way worse, but in the best way possible. Everything you think you know about the Capitol is actually ten times worse.

I literally read it in one sitting. I didn’t move from the couch all day and even read while eating. And I was in tears by the end.

8/10

The title definitely holds true. The ideas aren’t brand new, but the book frames them in totally new ways. This was my second time reading it, and obviously more of it stuck, especially if you’re into the whole “harsh reality” of things (which I am sometimes). I gave it an 8/10 because it’s well-written and thought-provoking, even if I didn’t agree with everything.
Favorite essay: #36

If you’re interested, I wrote more about essay #12 on my blog about the knowing-doing gap.

6/10

The ending with James and the last call actually made me cry, but overall I’d give it a 6. The plot was okay, focusing on Julie’s life after Sam’s death. I’m lucky not to have experienced true grief yet, so while I know it’s inevitable, I’m not sure I’m built for that kind of deep pain. Julie’s grieving felt real but didn’t dive too deep, so it didn’t fully hit me or have the same impact it might for someone going through loss. Still, it’s a sweet story for anyone dealing with grief.

7.5/10

The ending was bittersweet. I liked the storyline and the title was intriguing, but it could have been developed more. Joseph’s time with Jack’s family was detailed but didn’t have much impact. I wish we learned more about his time in juvie, his dad, or his journey with Madeline. The ending felt rushed, and it would have been nice to see Jupiter’s perspective later or switch between Jack’s and Madeline’s viewpoints.

8/10
I reread Hatchet after eight years because it randomly came to mind. It was the first book that ever made me sob, especially when the pilot died. Although some quotes hit a bit too bluntly for my taste, I still love them.

“…he learned the most important rule of survival, which was that feeling sorry for yourself didn’t work.”

“You are your most valuable asset. Don’t forget that. You are the best thing you have.”

10/10

10/10

This is a powerful reminder to notice the everyday things we usually overlook. Using the story of two fish unaware of the water around them, Wallace challenges us to step out of autopilot and choose how we see the world. I wrote more about how this speech resonated with me during a high school class (and later again in a college class) in my blog post here: (about water).

9.5/10

7/10

I gave the Harry Potter series a 7 out of 10. I binge-read all the books in a week, and while I enjoyed the magical world and characters, some parts felt dragged out or overhyped. It was fun to experience but didn’t totally wow me like I expected.

9/10

Beyond the action, it’s a sharp look at power, control, and survival. The Capitol’s use of media feels all too real, and Katniss’s struggle is about more than just survival, it’s about identity and resisting oppression. The story digs into trauma, morality, and inequality in a way that stuck with me long after reading.

6.5/10

Congrats on making it to the end! I definitely read way more in middle school, but unfortunately I’ve forgotten all of it — plus, you’ve probably already read those books anyway. You know the gist.

If you’ve got any recs for me though, send them my way 🙂

quotes.title: quotes
quotes.text:
words i live by 

“Where there’s a will there’s a way”

— Proverb 

“Don’t get too busy making a living that you forget to make a life.”

— Dolly Parton

“The walls of a person’s heart are not impregnable, not if they have ever known love.”

— Sunrise on the Reaping by Suzanne Collins

“The fool who knows he is a fool is much wiser.” 

— Buddha 

“Believe you can, then you will.” 

— Mulan 

“In the end, the love you take is equal to the love you make.” 

— Paul McCartney

“Not everyday is a good day, but there’s something good in every day.” 

— Alice Morse Earle

“Don’t let anyone tell you ‘no’. Do it with conviction, do it with passion, and you’ll find a way.” 

— Amanda Tapping

“You cannot read experience.” 

— Jafar

“Choose your hard.” 

“The more you do, the more you know. Increase the surface area of your life.” 

Do the best you can until you know better. Then when you know better, do better.” 

— Maya Angelou 

“There are far, far better things ahead than any we leave behind.” 

— C.S. Lewis 

“The secret to having a good life is knowing you already have one.”

“What we give doesn’t always return, but what we give is always what we are.” 

“Regret is unprofessional.” 

Rules for life or whatnot: 

Rule #1: Know that you are not special. 

Rule #2: Keep close anyone who disagrees with Rule #1. 

— some adulting book or another 

“Do it, or don’t. You’ll regret both.” 

“You like because, and you love despite.” 

— Set it Up

home.title: home
home.text:
“What is done with love is done well.”

Vincent Van Gogh 

That quote is probably in my top 4 favorite quotes (here’s the rest of the favorites). It’s something that I live by almost every day. This website is a collection of the things that I’ve done with love—art I’ve made, things I’ve written, places I’ve been, books that stuck with me, people I care about, and all the random things I’ve gotten curious about along the way. It’s a little gallery of my life and the things that make it meaningful. Thanks for stopping by! Click on each to learn more.

Welcome to The Riva Gallery.

A collection of personal, functional art. Pieces made to be used, worn, or just make a space feel a little more you. 
Aka “art made to be lived with”. 

My blog! This is a space for thoughts that don’t quite fit anywhere else into what I do—musings on life, little joys, heartbreaks, questions, and all the in-betweens. Think of it like a digital journal, open to anyone who might need it.

A growing archive of books I’ve read—some life-changing, some recommendations, or ones I just liked a lot (or ones I really didn’t). 

From handmade souvenirs to filmed memories, this is a record of the places I’ve been and the small things I noticed while I was there.
